utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good afternoon to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. I see that more or less everyone is present. If there are problems with interpretation, just let me know, please. Prosecution is Mr. Thayer is here and Mr. McCloskey. No significant absences from the Defence teams. All right. Mr. Thayer, no preliminaries, I take it, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. No -- no preliminaries. Okay. So Mr. Popovic will be represented now by Mr. Zivanovic, Major, and Mr. Zivanovic is going to cross-examine you first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Van Duijn, I'm going to direct your attention now to the 12th of July, 1995, when you found yourself at Potocari and when you and your soldiers helped when Muslim civilians were entering buses. I would like to ask you to look at a photograph that you already looked at yesterday. This is photograph 1516, and I would like you to tell us where you and your soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At which time, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the photograph would need to be rotated. Perhaps it can stay like this but I think it's actually the other way round. I think that's how we looked at it yesterday. This is how it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I would prefer to have it as it is now, from north to south.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we helped the Muslim refugees and tried to provide as much as humanitarian aid as possible, we were on a location that I can't see on this size, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you marked that yesterday, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With the words "refugees."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And we were just a little bit north of the area I marked as the refugee area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was marked yesterday, Mr. Zivanovic. Do you wish him to mark it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that yesterday he said where he arrived on the 12th of July, from position 02, but he didn't explicitly say that he remained at that position during the actual evacuation of Srebrenica. There is why I put this question. I recall him marking the place where he came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are 100 per cent right and that's why a minute ago or so, I asked you to be more specific, because he has already described to us that he started in one place but ended up in another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So can we zoom out a little bit on this photo, please? I think that's fine as it is now. Major, if you could kindly mark on this map or on this aerial image the various areas, sites, where you happened to be on the 12th of July, 1995. Starting from the one you marked yesterday as refugees, and then proceed as you like. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This first area I marked is basically the refugee area. The second one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could write again "refugees" next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm trying to assist you, Mr. Zivanovic, not to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second area is the area of the house with the lawn, where at the 12th the men were gathered, the men that were singled out, and basically my position on the 12th, from the morning I came from the position just a little bit north from point 02, I walked up to the area just in between of those two areas. That's where my personal position was at the 12th, and my men, the UNPROFOR men, were also in that position and among the refugees in the refugee area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So could you put LVD next -- those are your initials, okay. Thank you. Were you in any other place on that day, which would be included in this aerial image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- at the end of the day, I walked back to the compound so the road to the compound of DutchBat was also the area where I walked up and down, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From the -- on the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only, yeah, the main roads, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Back to you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at the same location on the 13th of July as well, the one that you've just marked?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, during the night, Lieutenant Koster assisted by making the V-shaped tunnel a little bit more to the north, so basically up to the location I was during the 12th. So my position on the 13th was just a little bit more to the north, more to the area of the house with the lawns in front of them but basically the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us how many UNPROFOR soldiers besides you assisted the refugees?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have to make an estimation now, depending on the day and depending on the time, varying between 30 and 40 soldiers from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned the letter V, are you saying that this V was formed actually by soldiers or by the UN vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By use of the UN vehicles, you can see in the video that the APCs are positioned in such a way that resembles more or less the V shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the total number of APCs was that you had at your disposal there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The APCs that we used to make the V shape were four APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You arrived there in accordance with the instructions of your superior. I think his name is Groen. And I think that he had the rank of captain. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th and the 13th of July, were you in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 12th, I was still under the command of Captain Groen. By the time I went to the refugee area, Captain Groen withdrew with the rest of his company that was originally based in Srebrenica town, in the compound there, and from that moment on, I was directly placed under the battalion command, so the battalion operations room, and there was no direct link between me and Captain Groen anymore. So from that moment on, from the time I came at the position of the refugee area, I was directly under battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the battalion command, could you mention the name of the officer under whose command you were?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During those two days, did you receive any orders from him to do anything else other than what you were actually doing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those two days, I did not have a personal contact with him. The contacts were through the duty officer at the operations room, or with Major Franken. That was the second in command of the battalion. And of course I spoke with Major Franken to see what the things were that we could do to adjust the situation, but there were no big changes to the things we did there at that time, at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any instructions from Major Franken or from the duty officers to do anything else other than what you were doing anyway?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Van Duijn, yesterday you said that at the beginning, when you came to Potocari and when the transport of the refugees began, the men were not separated from the rest, at the beginning. Could you please tell me how long this lasted?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly if the men were separated from the beginning on. As I stated, I did not see or notice or did not get any reports that they were singled out from the beginning on, but if I have to make an estimation, I think that would be the first order -- the first two hours of the transports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, does that mean that there was no separation of the men during the first two hours of the transport?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I have ever seen or did I get any reports about that. I don't know if it didn't happen. I only know that after those first one or two hours, I got reports and I saw myself that the men were singled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Quite a large number of vehicles passed by you, vehicles in which these refugees were transported, trucks, buses. Did you see if any of those buses or trucks stopped to refill gas?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that this was done at a location that was a little bit more to the north in relation to where you were?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you also spoke about a suspension of the transport on the 12th of July. You said that in the evening, Serb soldiers went to Bratunac to celebrate. Did they perhaps tell you that this was an important Orthodox holiday, St. Peter's Day, and that that was the reason why they went to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell me that. They just told me that they went to Bratunac to Hotel Fontana to celebrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During that night, you didn't have an opportunity to see any Serbian soldiers where you were?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was -- sorry. At that time, I was at the compound of DutchBat and there were no Serbian soldiers at the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were more to the north in the Dutch Battalion's base, but before you got to the base, did you happen to see perhaps Serbian soldiers around the compound, in the yard around the base?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian soldiers I had seen when I went from the location of the refugee area to the DutchBat compound were the soldiers that took part in the roll-call I saw at the evening of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You did talk about that. Thank you. On the 13th of July, you said that without the presence of the Serbian soldiers, a number of refugees were dispatched in buses in the direction of Muslim territory, and of course when this was done, you did not carry out any separations. Could you please tell us how many men approximately left at that time in the buses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be very difficult to calculate. I can make an estimation now, and if I have to do that, then I would think of maybe 100 or 150 Muslim men that we could keep with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the Serb soldiers came on the 13th of July, around 8.30 in the morning, you continued to work in the same way that you did the day before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing changed because of the fact that you had previously sent this group of Muslims off in the buses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Serbian soldiers came to that location again, to my location at the 13th, from that moment on, the singling out of the men started again. And because of course by the Serbian soldiers, this happened, this was the same way as it happened at the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered the question, Major. The question was: "Nothing changed because of the fact that you had previously sent this group of Muslims off in the buses?" That was the question. In other words, as I read Mr. Zivanovic's question, the fact that you had succeeded in sending some -- a group of men together with their families off in the buses before the arrival of the Serb soldiers did not have any repercussion on what happened afterwards, did it? This is basically what you're being asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no repercussions for me or for the way DutchBat worked. We worked in the same vein as on the 12th. The only difference was the singling out by the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that answer your question, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us yesterday that once the refugees left Potocari on the 13th of July, 1995, they left behind quite a lot of their personal items; amongst other things, you mentioned photographs, blankets. My question is whether other than photographs, blankets, you saw identification documents, identity cards, passports, drivers's licences, weapons permits, and similar documents.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Passports I had seen were on the lawn of the "White House" and if I'm not mistaken, the other photographs and blankets which I talked about yesterday were the personal items that were left behind in the refugee area. In the refugee area I saw blankets, photographs. I didn't see specifics in the sense of passports in the refugee area. The passports I had seen were on the lawn of the "White House."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And identity cards? And drivers's licences, weapons permits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I have not seen that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Muslim refugees, I saw no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. No, I didn't mean the refugees. I meant amongst the items that were left behind after the refugees departed.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke about the blocking positions which you took up before the fall of Srebrenica on the 10th of July, that you and your unit assumed. Could you please tell us whether these blocking positions were on the road between Srebrenica and Zelani Jadar?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Zelani Jadar is, so I couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many APCs were used in the taking up of this -- or these blocking positions?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, the one I know about that were under the control of Captain Groen, there were six APCs on different locations. Near my location and as I stated before, the night of the 9th and the 10th I left with two APCs. But in total, there were six, what I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did perhaps when you were returning to Srebrenica come a time when one of your APCs slid off the road?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one of my APCs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are not aware of any such thing, you didn't see that APC, or do you mean that that APC was not under your command?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not an APC that was under my command slid off the road, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure you understood me. I was asking if you were aware that any of the APCs of the UN, no matter under whose command, slid off the road on the way back to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the way back to Srebrenica, I haven't heard of one of the APCs sliding off the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long was your return trip to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean coming back from the blocking position to the compound or to point 02?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the return trip you mentioned in your last answer.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the return trip, that's what I meant, coming back from the APCs north to the compound of -- of the battalion in -- at the base in Potocari, that's -- was beginning on the 11th and lasted more or less the whole day until the starting of the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. I meant your return from the blocking position to Srebrenica, the blocking position that you held on the 10th of July. How long did it take you to go back to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 10th on, I took up the blocking position, and on the 11th, we pulled back gradually towards the base of the Bravo Company which is located in the centre of Srebrenica. So that took the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To return from the blocking position to the centre of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another thing you said yesterday was that UN convoys were restricted - I mean humanitarian convoys - and that was especially felt in March and April 1995. Do you know why these restrictions occurred?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Serbs, and the Serb forces did not grant the permission for the convoys to enter and there were two types of convoys, purely humanitarian convoys for the refugees in the area and the convoys for us to be resupplied, meaning DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But do you know why the convoys were prevented from entering, why restrictions were imposed on them? Have you heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reason why the Serb forces did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That shortage was certainly felt by you and your soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you that you could ask your superior officers, for instance, why you were not getting the things that you needed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and we spoke about that constantly. And the explanation was that the Serb forces did not get the clearance, give the clearance, needed for the convoys to get in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not ask your superior officers whether the Serb forces provided any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the explanation, no clearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in contact with Serb forces yourself, Serb armed forces, the Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask them perhaps why you were not allowed access to the things you needed so badly, such as food?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We spoke about that and also about regional aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did they tell you why the UN convoys were restricted?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that they gave me any explanation other than that they didn't know why the convoys were not granted with the clearance. The clearances were given on another post, post near OP-Papa called Yellow Bridge, and that was not in my area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I think this needs a little bit of a clarification. It's too generic the way you've put the question, Mr. Zivanovic. At the time, Major, you were a lieutenant and platoon commander, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you've just stated that you or you accepted the proposition that you were in contact with Serb forces. This is how it was put to you. And you said yes, that's correct. And then you added that or you spoke about the matter of -- the matter that we are talking about, with these Serb forces but can you be specific? What do you mean by "Serb forces"? Were you speaking to persons in command, to ordinary military soldiers, to officers, to generals, to commanders or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near to one of my observation posts in my area, OP Romeo, there was a bunker of Serb forces just outside of the enclave, and the group commander on OP Romeo was into regular contact with the Serb soldiers there in that bunker, and I myself also during the six months was into contact with them on a few occasions, and then of course we spoke about the things, the regional aspects, the border line incidents that had happened during weeks before, and we also spoke about of course the lack of resupplying that we faced. But there were no commanders or other high positioned Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question on this subject. Did any of the people you were in contact with tell you on the subject of restrictions imposed on humanitarian aid that the reason why the convoys were restricted is that part of that humanitarian aid is going to the Muslim armed forces in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm objecting at this point as opposed to a couple of times ago because this question has been asked in several different forms and he's answered consistently that he didn't receive any specific information from any Serb forces as to the reason for the restriction on the various supply convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead and answer the question, but this will be the last time this matter is being addressed, unless there are really different approaches to it. Major, I'm allowing the question after having consulted with my colleagues for the simple reason that it's specific to the people that you were in contact with. It's not as generic as the others were. This is very specific. So limiting yourself to the people that you were in contact with. You've just described who they were. During your conversations or exchanges on the subject of restrictions, were you told or were you informed by any of them that the reason why the convoys were restricted is that or was that part of the humanitarian aid was going to the Muslim armed forces in the enclave? Do you recall ever having been told this by any of the Serbs military that you conversed with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just two more questions on the previous subject regarding your return from the blocking position to Srebrenica. Can you tell us how far were they from the town?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending how you would describe the town, basically our positions were in the outskirts of Srebrenica, on the south side, and so basically we were still in the region of Srebrenica, and the drawback that we did happened in phases, so it is difficult to make an estimation now, but I would think a few kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. We do appreciate very much the fact that you single yourself out and stick to the time indicated previously for cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we need to do this. Mr. Zivanovic? You might hear me better. I suppose that you want to save this image with the markings of -- So Major, could you be kind enough to sign it, please? And then Madam Registrar will immortalise it in the records of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then it will be given a number later on when you tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Defence for Mr. Beara. Mr. Meek, Christopher Meek, will be cross-examining you, Major, now on behalf of Colonel Beara. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, thank you very much, but on behalf of Mr. Beara, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much, Mr. Meek. Defence for Mr. Nikolic? Mr. Stephane Bourgon, who is defending together with Madam Nikolic, accused Nikolic will be cross-examining you now. You had indicated 30 minutes as an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major. I only have a few questions for you as the client I represented was not involved in the activities you testified about. Now, in your testimony, you were asked many questions concerning your knowledge of the Bosnian Serb army. And in this regard, would you agree with me that during the time of your tour, that is from January to July, that the information that was available to you and to DutchBat concerning the structure and organisation of the Bosnian Serb army was limited to what you had received prior to your deployment?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the reason for this is that your battalion, DutchBat, that is, either did not have intelligence gathering capability or did not use such capability during the six months that you were there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: DutchBat tried to use everything it had when it comes to intelligence gathering. But you're correct when it comes to intelligence outside the enclave, we did not have any support or means of ourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during your testimony you were asked some questions about an individual you referred to as being Major Nikolic. Now, I take it from your responses to the questions by my colleague from the Prosecution, that Major Nikolic was well known to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you in a position to confirm that Major Nikolic was indeed a key player in the events which took place on the 12th and 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was a key player. I can only say what I have seen during those two days and of course the days before, and that was that Major Nikolic was also on site and was into contact with people that I had seen at the site and know that they had a key role in the events on those two days, meaning Mane and Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it was your understanding talking about these two individuals, that Major Nikolic was the superior to Stalin who in turn was the superior to Mane?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, I hate this when it happens; however, we have a technical problem. And I'm told that outside the courtroom the synchronisation between image and sound has gone bust. So it needs to be taken care of, and I've been asked to grant a short break and they will attend to the matter. It doesn't affect us in here but it does affect outside. 30 minutes you need? All right. So we will have a 30-minute break, ensuring that in the meantime this will be sorted out and then we continue afterwards. Thank you. --- Break taken at 3.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is everything fixed? All right. Thank you. My apologies again to you, Mr. Bourgon, and to you, Major. You can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Major. I only have a few more questions for you. The first one dealing with your knowledge of the person I represent in this case. I have read all of your material related to your testimony and prior testimony, and I would just like to confirm or -- whether -- to ask you to confirm that during your tour in Bosnia, you never came across or heard of anyone by the name of Second Lieutenant Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would like to you confirm also in the same way that you never came across or heard of anyone referred to as the security officer or chief of security of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never heard about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, then again, if I ask you whether you are aware that Zvornik Brigade was one of the brigades within the Drina Corps, are you or were you able at the time to confirm this?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time also after preparing for the mission, I had a fairly good idea of the Serb units that were in the area, and I've heard the name of the Zvornik Brigade in combination with that area, but that's the only thing I can say about that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my last question, or a couple of questions, deal with your knowledge of the man you describe or you identified - sorry - as being General Mladic. Now, on the basis of your personal experience, would you agree with me that General Mladic was a charismatic leader who knew very well how to make his presence felt?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has some sort of dark form of charisma, and he makes sure by using his body-guards in such a way that everyone knows that he's present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And Major, even though you are not from the same army as General Mladic, and although you are -- you know you're taller than General Mladic, would you agree with me that meeting him on those two occasions was somewhat of an intimidating experience?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really for me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer you quickly to your testimony in the Blagojevic case. Do you remember having testified in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in that case, you were asked to describe the demeanour of General Mladic both times you met him. And your answer, and I quote here from the transcript in the Blagojevic case, on page 1114, that is 1114. And your answer was as follows: "He was giving orders when he wanted to, but the process was ongoing, and like in every army, when the highest ranking officer comes to the scene and he wants to change anything, he can because he's the commander." Do you still agree with what you said in the Blagojevic case? Would you still agree with that today?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is the correct sentence, but if you -- as you read it, I still agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We now come to the Defence of Mr. Borovcanin, and it's Mr. Lazarevic who will be cross-examining you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Van Duijn. [Interpretation] Major, I should like to establish first on how many occasions you testified, whether before the military bodies, Dutch state organs and this Tribunal. In fact, the first thing you did was fill in a questionnaire for the purposes of the ICTY. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember filling in questionnaires, but I don't recall which questionnaire was aimed or meant to be for which body.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Would it assist you if I showed you the questionnaire? I have a hard copy here, if you just want to see whether it's that document. It's four pages long.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has this been scanned, Mr. Lazarevic or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was just trying to establish whether it was his handwriting and when whether he really filled in this questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's put it on the ELMO, please, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the questionnaire I filled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell me, since I did not manage to find the date on this questionnaire, if you remember when you filled it in?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall when I filled this questionnaire in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't need it on the ELMO anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal on the 25th October, 1995. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the statement which was in Assen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it's a statement you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal. The date on it is the 25th of October, 1995. Do we have any reason to doubt that? Do you want me to show you the document?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, I remember this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also gave a statement to the Royal Army of the Netherlands titled "Operative processing of Srebrenica, debriefing." Can you tell me when you made a debriefing before the Royal Army of the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please show me that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] By all means.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the translation of the debriefing that was also held in Assen. And on the Dutch version, as I remember correctly, if I remember correctly, the dates are on that, but I don't remember from the top of my mind when this debriefing was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, you do not contest that you gave that statement and that is the translation of that statement?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Also according to the information we received from the OTP, you gave another statement in the process of debriefing on the 12th and 13th September 1995. It is a slightly longer statement, 20 pages long. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please see that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the whole personal statement I made in Assen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So that is that statement. And after that, in 2002, on the 11th November, you testified here in The Hague before the Parliamentary Commission of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the date but I was a witness in that parliamentary inquiry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You can take my word for it or you can see the date on the document.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And just in conclusion, you have already testified in this Tribunal, in the Krstic case, the Blagojevic and Jokic case. That is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, having looked through all your statements together, can you tell me if there may be yet another statement that you may have given to either military bodies or the state bodies of the Netherlands, the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, or anything else, any statement at all that I'm not aware of?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say if there is another statement. This seems to be all the statements I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. When giving all these statements in the process of debriefing, before the Parliamentary Commission, and during testimony, you always spoke the truth to the best of your recollection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, when you came to testify, and during proofing, did Mr. Thayer, the person I know did the proofing with you, show you these statements that I have just shown you myself?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to review those statements, to familiarise yourself with the contents, or maybe make corrections as to the accuracy of some statements or correct some typographical errors, such as in the dates, such as from the 13th July 1995 to the 14th July 1995? Did you have occasion to do that during your proofing session with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you this: So you familiarised yourself with your statements, you reviewed them, you made your corrections. Now, do you stand by everything that you stated, asserted, in those statements?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like this document to be shown to the witness. Unfortunately, I don't have it on the e-court so I will have to use the ELMO for this. We were unfortunately late to put this document in the e-court system, but I believe that this will work fine with the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Van Duijn, during your testimony yesterday, I understood that on your APC you took up position, blocking position, at location 02 and from that position you saw the arrival of the members of the army of Republika Srpska. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of my testimony was slightly different, because at first we took up a position at point 02. Later on because the shelling was too heavy on point 02, we took up a position later on that day, on the 11th, a little bit north of point 02, but from that location we could see point 02, the crossroads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I accept fully what you've just said. Could you please look now at this document that is on the ELMO? We received it from the Office of the Prosecutor, and you have already marked position 02 on it. The point circled in the bottom part of that picture, is that point 02?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This point I marked now is the crossroads as we called 02, point 02.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's how I understood this drawing of yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, Madam Usher, if you could kindly give the witness a coloured pen, any colour. And if he could kindly draw around the same circle that he indicated to us a minute ago, put your -- the description 02.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point 02. And could you just initial that area, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please mark the other position that you moved to or withdrew to after you left position 02?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be just a little bit north of point 02. Must have been in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Zoom out a little bit further. Further. Can I see the handwriting down -- zoom, zoom out. Further. Yes. Point 02 and further can I see -- usher, yeah, further down, yes. What does it -- what is it? Is it your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can explain, Your Honour, this is the sketch which I made myself. The position of the APCs at point 02 where we positioned ourself at first and later on, we only were there for a few hours, and later on we positioned our APCs a little bit more north, with two APCs on each side of the road so it was easier, but this was a sketch to make clear in the operational or in the debrief to show where our APCs were at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the rest of the handwriting on the page, on the sides, is it yours as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the handwriting in the bottom, and the handwriting on the sides is from the interviewers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this second circle that you drew, which more or less represents the position to which you withdrew from position 02, so can you mark that as the second position? Can you please do that with a marker?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now this place where we have written down "second position," that is the place where you saw the arrival of the Serbian forces, the forces of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the position where I spent the night from the 11th in the evening, where also the arrival of Sergeant Mulder of OP Mike was and consequently in the morning of the 12th, the arrival of the Serb forces. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you talked about Serbian forces arriving from two different directions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark with an arrow the first direction that the Serbian forces arrived from? The first units that arrived from the first direction or one of the directions.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first Serb soldiers we saw crossing the fields on the eastern side, and then came on the road at point 02. After clearing the houses there, they came up to the north to our location. I hope this is visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The arrow that you just drew shows the direction from which the Serbian forces arrived. Is that the same direction where the observation posts Romeo and Quebec were? Did they arrive from that direction?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Romeo and Quebec were in the northeast but were further away. From the reports we got, troops, Serbian troops, came alongside the compound in Potocari, on the eastern side, then crossed the fields and then came up to the road. When you look at the reports, it should be those troops that crossed the fields after being on the eastern side of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Can you please now sketch in these other Serb forces that you saw with an arrow? What was the other direction where these other Serbian forces came from?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. The other forces came from the north, on the road from north to south.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now if you can write next to the arrows "VRS" so that we know what they stand for.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be more precise, after this last VRS that you wrote, could you put -- add the number 1, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And at the end of the previous one, yeah, could you put a number 2, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question and I think then we will not be needing this map anymore, but the question is actually not so specifically related to the map. What was the time that this happened? When was it that you saw these Serbian forces? Could you please be more specific about the time when you saw this happening?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the morning of the 12th, and it must have been around 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't need this map anymore. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The night of the 11th and 12th of July you spent at that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position just north of point 02, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. And that night, according to our information, at around quarter past 12.00, or after midnight, a large group of refugees, a large group of people, passed by these positions of yours. And I think you described that.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my recollection, it was a little bit before midnight, around 11.00, 11.00 or 12.00, but that was the group of Sergeant Mulder coming -- accompanied by a large group of refugees coming from the area around OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's not so important whether it was a quarter of an hour, 20 minutes earlier or an hour later. What I'm interested in is that large group of refugees that passed by. Did you notice people with weapons in that group of people?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Major, in your testimony yesterday, you mentioned several times Captain Mane. Specifically on page 52 of the transcript you said that you told you that the refugees would be transported out of the enclave and that he wanted to know whether the UN soldiers would stay or would go back to the base. So he practically provided you with an opportunity, either of staying there or returning to the UN base. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And while we are on the subject of Captain Mane, you recognised him on the stills, the video footage, and it was evident from your testimony that you had many contacts with him. Did you notice if he was wearing any rank insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any rank insignia on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he was a captain by rank, or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He told me himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He personally told you. Thank you. At the point when Captain Mane informed you or actually asked you whether you wanted to stay where you were or if you wanted to return to the base, you decided to stay. What I'm interested in is if this decision was something that you made yourself or whether you consulted any of your superiors in reaching this decision.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I took this decision myself because it was also in line with earlier guidelines of our battalion command to only provide humanitarian aid, and I thought at that time it was the best way to do that by staying there at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's what I understood also, that it was your personal decision, and I accept that. When you continued with your testimony yesterday, and this is on page 53 of the transcript, lines 9 to 12, you said that you were in contact with Major Franken and that you heard from him that he also was aware of the fact that the refugees would be transported and that's when it practically became clear to you that this would actually happen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my contacts with Major Franken, he confirmed that he had also heard, in talks, that this was the case and that the refugees were supposed to be transported out of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So Major Franken already knew this when you called him. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. Basically he was surprised that it was already happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So from this, from your reply, can we conclude that the agreement on the evacuation of the refugees was achieved at a much higher level than your level and the level of Captain Mane, who were actually there at the actual location?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was any agreement of the sort. What was clear that not only on my level but also on a higher level, there were talks about the evacuation of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I accept that you perhaps don't know all the details about who reached the agreement, when the agreement was reached. Are you aware that Colonel Karremans had meetings with General Mladic, that they discussed the topic, that there were some meetings at the Hotel Fontana where some of these things were agreed on and discussed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware at that time of any meetings because basically I was too busy with my own dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I understand from your answer that you found out about this but probably this was later, through the media, or by reading the NIOD reports or in another way.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read about it later, but I don't recall any agreement of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's how I understood your answer. At one point in your testimony yesterday, you mentioned that you were - I'm going to use the same term that you used in your testimony - a human chain, in order to attempt to calm down the refugees so that they would not be overcome by panic. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood it properly, based on your testimony in other cases, it seems that there was a stampede by the refugees which happened shortly before you arrived, where people crushed each other in an attempt to come to the front, so I assume that that was probably the reason why you set up this human chain. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also heard about some sort of a stampede but it was clear to me that we needed to form that human chain in order to prevent people to crush each other or if they would fall down that someone, the other people would stand on them. So that was the reason why we organised it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As we were looking at the video footage that we were shown and based on statements by others, there was not only the human chain that was formed there but there were also some coloured tapes that were physically separating the refugees from the Serbian soldiers. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've also seen that on the video footage but that was before I came to that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't know who actually set up these -- this tape, because you weren't there at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Once you arrived, could you please say what the distance was in metres between the refugees and the first Serb soldiers who were there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically the soldiers, Serb soldiers that were the closest to the refugees were Mane and Miki, because they were with me, and we were standing more or less 20, 25 metres behind my soldiers that formed the human chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mane and Miki were thus standing right next to you while the other soldiers were about 20 or 25 metres away. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at a very brief segment of the video footage that has already been shown here marked V0003914. [In English] The 65 ter number is P02007.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It starts at 19.34 and it goes to 19.50. There are only some 15 seconds of this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What we've just seen in this segment, is that this buffer zone where your soldiers were and the refugees were on one side of it and the Serbian soldiers were on the other side of it? This is what we were just talking about. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This piece of film is just -- must have been around the time I arrived there, so it was not exactly the way it was organised but it resembles it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: When I was looking at this footage, I noticed the DutchBat soldiers, they all had weapons, based on what I could see on the footage. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've also seen it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've already responded to a question by my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic about the time when you first noticed the separation of men from the rest of the refugees began. I have one more thing to ask you about that. You said that Mane, Captain Mane, informed you that the reason the men were being separated was to check whether there were war criminals among them, based on a list that they had, and I quoted your testimony page 54 of the transcript, lines 21 to 24. What I'm interested now specifically is this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown document 4 D15? Unfortunately the translation of this document is still pending, although it is tendered into evidence a while ago. We had some problems with translation. But I will try to translate as much as I can. Maybe I would rather read it out in B/C/S because this is a list of names, and I'm interested only the headline of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed the way you have just suggested, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major, there is a document here in B/C/S with the following heading: "List of war criminals known to the command of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade who committed war crimes in the territory of the municipalities of Bratunac, Srebrenica, Milici, Vlasenica and Skelani, who are believed to be in Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page, the bottom of the second page because it has a date of this document. It's one page before this one. The next one. And another one? Well, my case manager just informed me that it's the last-but-one -- second by last. Okay. We have a date now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see here at the end of the document, it says "Bratunac, 12th of July 1995"? Did you ever see this document before?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Based on the title of the document and the list of the people on it and the date of the document, can we not conclude that it confirms precisely what Captain Mane told you, that there was a list of suspected war criminals and that is what you actually found out from Mane, that there is such a list?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this list, but if the date is correct, then it seems to confirm what Mane told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In your testimony yesterday, you mentioned an incident involving a soldier in a black uniform and who tried to pull out a young man from a group of refugees who was -- he tried to pull him out, having grabbed his throat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was unclear, though, from what you said yesterday whether Captain Mane managed to stop this soldier from doing what he was doing and to make him leave the area where the refugees were.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I answer there question, can I please have the transcript in my screen? Because I only have the list on both screens. Thank you. I have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher is going to assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've read it. Thank you. Captain Mane stopped the soldier and removed him from the site at my request, and the boy was kept with his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So like in numerous situations before that, Captain Mane acknowledged your request and acted accordingly?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to choose the moments to do the requests, but every time I did a request with Captain Mane, he backed me up and the men were able to stay with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning this man who tried to drag away that boy, you said he had a black uniform, different from the uniforms worn by Mane and his soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude from that that this man in the black uniform did not belong to Captain Mane's unit?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The uniforms were more or less combined. But his overall or black uniform was different than from the other combined uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But Major, you saw the lineup of the unit commanded by Mane. The man in black was not in that lineup, was he?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Major, before you took the stand, another member of the DutchBat testified, then major now Colonel Boering, and he confirmed that the embarkation of refugees on to buses took place on several locations, not just one. In your experience; is that correct? I'm talking about the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't object to the substance of the question per se, but I believe we've had some rulings in this regard with respect to identifying the names of particular witnesses who testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness has -- I think it's a harmless question. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know of any information. I don't have any information that the embarkation of the refugees took place on several locations. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But generally speaking, on the 12th of July, did you see Major Boering in that area where men were being singled out around that house where the men were placed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of meeting Major Boering at that day, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. Based on the markings you made on the aerial photograph yesterday, I understood that the refugees were not only in the area that you secured but also in the building of the UN base itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also refugees in the building at the UN compound, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It follows from your testimony that you spent the night of the 12th in the compound. Did you see the refugees there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that. I just went into the compound, spoke with my commander and with Major Franken, and after that, I went straight to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but from your previous answer, I understood that you were aware the refugees were also on the premises of the UN compound. But you mean to say that when you came in, you didn't see them or you were certain perhaps that they had already left?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From what I can remember now, the night of the 12th and the 13th, there were still refugees on the camp. I only don't remember seeing them there at that specific night.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps who secured the evacuation of that group of refugees, the ones who were in the compound?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Before you went on leave to the UN compound, you saw Mane's unit lining up and leaving; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall a lining up of Mane's unit. I saw Mane's unit leaving, like Mane told me. After that I went to the compound, and on that way I saw the roll-call I mentioned about with Stalin, the person Stalin, heading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's what I meant, but they did leave, in any event, because on the next day, when you came, they were no longer there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you observe if any unit of the army of Republika Srpska remained in Potocari overnight?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen that and I didn't hear any report from Lieutenant Koster about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And of course, you have no information that any of the VRS soldiers came into the UN compound and moved among the refugees during that night?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any information about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you another document now, a Defence document. [In English] 4 D17. It's also on B/C/S pending translation. Yes. That's the document. [Interpretation] I suppose you do not understand the language but let me tell you what is written there, and the interpreters are always here to confirm. In the left-hand corner it says: "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, army General Staff." The number of the document is indicated, date, 12th July 1995. And it says it was either sent or received at 1325 hours, and it is addressed to the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, via the 1st Corps command, commanded by Brigade General Mustafa Hajrulahovic Talijan [In English] the signature and the stamp. [Interpretation] The author of this document is Chief of Staff, Brigade General Enver Hadzihasanovic. Can we now move back to page 1, please? So, I'm interested in one sentence in particular. It reads: "They organised an attack at Potocari. Tonight, around 2300 hours, we had 15 to 20.000 refugees who were sitting in the area of combat activities, together with 300 fighters of the BH army on the camp in Potocari." I suppose that you did not have an opportunity to see this document before. But this reference to 300 combatants of the BH army in the camp at Potocari, is it consistent with your experience, at least in terms of the number? Is it possible, likely correct, that among the men who were there, there were 300 combatants?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before, but the numbers that are mentioned, also the 15 to 20.000 refugees on the camp, seems -- and also the 300 fighters of the BH army seems incorrect to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But if we look at the number of men of military age, fit for the army that you saw there, you will agree that there were more than 300?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen men or any other refugees during the night on the 12th or the 13th, and I don't recall that they were fighters of the BH army. When you look at the total of men that I saw on the two days, and the men that were singled out, that must resemble more than 300, 350 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But in your book, as a professional soldier, what does this term "fighter" represent?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "fighter" is not frequently used. The term that is being used is "military man." And there are distinct definitions for that, like wearing a uniform and being in a military unit. So this is basically the definition of "military man." But the term "fighter" is not being used by me or in the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in that case, let's reformulate it. Let's say member of a military unit. You just said the outward signs of such a man are the uniform he wears and the weapon he carries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Dutch definition doesn't speak about a weapon but that could be part of a definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And if a Dutch soldier would discard his weapon, take off his uniform and put on civilian clothes, would he thereby cease to be a soldier of the Dutch army in an attempt to avoid capture?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would still be a soldier of the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is precisely what I wanted to know. One more point in regard to this document: This reference that there are some 300 fighting men among the civilians in Potocari, this information, it had to come from somewhere in the area, from the spot, from the 28th Division. How otherwise could have the -- could the 1st Corps command have found out about it, to inform the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And finally, I would like to take up one more subject that you covered in your testimony, the issue of passports. You said yesterday you found them on the lawn outside the "White House" and the passports belonged to the men seated inside the house. It's page 71, lines 11 through 16 in the transcript. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit 4 D36? It's in English version page 8, paragraph 8. Yes. And for the benefit of our clients, in B/C/S it's page 7, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is the statement you gave to the investigators of the ICTY. I have shown it to you before. You confirmed it was yours. The date is 25 October 1995. Please look at paragraph 8. It says: "[In English] Scattered all over the field near the bus station, I saw personal property belonging to the Muslim people. There were passports and other papers lying around everywhere." [Interpretation] You've already said that this statement you gave was true and correct and given to the best of your recollection, and you also said that you had no corrections to make except the ones that I have already mentioned. So you stand by this statement, that passports were lying in the field next to the bus station?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been my recollection at that time, that I also spoke about passports. At this time I don't have any recollection of seeing passports at the bus station area, only when we speak about the "White House." But it could also be something, when it comes to making up the report, which is not made by me but by the person that interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that something was put in your statement that you did not say?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any recollection of mentioning passports then, but it could be that my recollection then also meant passports. If I think back now, I don't remember any other passports than the passports that were in front of the lawn at the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This was in October 1995, when your memory was very fresh. It was just after the events. Do you agree that your recollection was better in 1995 than now, 11 years later?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be better then. It is true that the memory was fresher than it is now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to identify that location that we mentioned here, approximately how far is the bus station from the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is not more than 150, 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And that is on the other side of the asphalt road, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the opposite side than the side of the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we could conclude from this that passports --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, there seems to be some misunderstanding in the transcript. Did you say it was on the opposite side of the UN base or at the same side where the UN base was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's on the opposite side than the side of the UN compound. I'm speaking about the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand the "White House" was on the other side, but the question here was about the bus station. Was the bus station on the same side as the UN compound or not?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection, the bus station was on the same side as the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
