utterances.text: Yes. I agree. We just need to get that straight in the transcript. So we can conclude from this that those passports were scattered over a larger area, not only outside the "White House"? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be so that in other locations this were also passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday at one point that you collected the passports you found and put them in your pockets. Can you tell me approximately how many passports you gathered?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until my pockets were full, so that must have been 20 or 25 passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We have seen footage of you at that time wearing shorts and that seems to be the maximum number you could fit into your pockets. But when you picked up the passports, did you open them to see to whom they belonged?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've opened a few, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you opened some but not the 20 or the 25 you collected. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you opened the passports, were all the passport holders, so to say, men?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my recollection, that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. And these few passports that you did open belonged to men. Did you personally know any of them?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you did not know anyone. You did not enter the "White House" at any point, you didn't go in?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just had a look inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you looked inside without entering?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So when you looked inside, did you recognise anyone? Did any of the faces you saw -- I mean, were any of the faces you saw familiar?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you do not know the identity of the persons found inside the "White House" when you looked inside?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And your statement yesterday that the passports you found belonged to the men who were inside the "White House" is just your assumption, right? You do not know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember person telling me, I don't remember who it was, but that the personal belongings in front of the "White House" were in fact of the men in the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But you cannot claim that with any certainty because you don't know who the men inside the "White House" were and you don't know whose passports you held?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know that when I confronted Mane with the story about the passports is that he confirmed to me that the people inside the house did not need the passports anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to Mane but for the moment, I want to clarify this. You don't know whether the passports in your pockets, only several of which you actually opened, belonged to any of the men in the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered that. He told you that all he can tell is someone, he can't remember who, told him that. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just one more question in relation to these passports. You also cannot know if the persons from whose passports they were, threw away these passports themselves, lost them or perhaps were ordered by the Serbian soldiers to throw them away and that's what they did. So you were not there when these passports were actually discarded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. I was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. Major Van Duijn, we heard testimony here from certain Muslim witnesses who said that many amongst them threw away their personal documents in order to avoid being identified by the Serbian soldiers. Did you know about that? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. During your testimony yesterday, you said that at one point you asked Captain Mane about these passports and that he just frowned and said that they would no longer be needing the passports. And you practically repeated that just now. I would like us now to look once again at the statement you gave to the Prosecutor on the 25th of October, 1995. This is page 8, last paragraph, and the beginning of page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. I notice Mr. Thayer standing. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this may be a translation issue, but I don't believe that that accurately reflects the testimony that he gave yesterday with respect to Captain Mane's response to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is going to read out, however, from the transcript, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thought it was going to be a statement, not the testimony, Your Honour, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I actually first said -- I actually carried out -- well, I actually referred to the transcript of the 27th of September, on page 92, in order to just tell the witness when it was that he said that, but since the witness now again talked about this incident with the passports and Captain Mane, I just wanted to then go back to the statement of the 25th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can go, certainly can go back to the statement, if you want to, but please either make it available to the witness or, if it's a short excerpt, read it out slowly so that it can be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This document is already on the screen so perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Major Van Duijn, you see yourself the last paragraph of your statement, and it talks about your departure to the "White House." "[In English] At that moment I was standing about five metres away" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the end of page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It was too quick for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the last sentence of that -- of the last paragraph reads precisely that. "At that moment I was standing about five metres away from the house." And then do you want to move to page 9, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then on page 9, first paragraph. "I asked one of the soldiers if the men did not need their belongings anymore. He replied that the belongings were not longer needed. I did not ask any more question about this at the time, but I suspect that these men were killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement that you gave to the Prosecutor and which I just quoted to you suggests that you talked about this not with Captain Mane but with a soldier who is referred to here as another -- or one of the soldiers, one of the Serb soldiers. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time this statement was made up, the story about the passports was not as interesting or was not focused on in detail more than later on, so this is just some sort of a general overview over the incident as it happened at the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in 1995, in October, you already knew who Captain Mane was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And if I'm not mistaken, you mentioned him as Captain Mane at least 15 times in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor's Office; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not count the number of times, but I must be sure that -- I'm sure that I mentioned his name in the statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But here, in this part where you talked about your suspicion that those people would be killed, you said "one of the soldiers." You do not mention Captain Mane by name, do you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have named him during the interview but for one reason or another it's not in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the investigators of The Hague Tribunal who interviewed you would omit such an important detail, that it was Captain Mane that was being talked about? Or, rather, that you had said it was Captain Mane and that they had written down "one of the soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an explanation why this is in generic terms. I only know that later on in the process, the story about the passports and the "White House" was more focused on in detail and then all the names and details were spread out in other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, is it time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to point that out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I only have another 15 minutes, not more than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now. And then it's your turn, Madam Fauveau. How much time do you require? Initially you had indicated an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 45 minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So -- and after that, I don't think we'll finish today anyway, which means you'll need to come again tomorrow but I promise you it will all be over tomorrow. So 25 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Van Duijn, you know where we left off, more or less, but during the break my attention was drawn to the fact that some things were not quite clear in the transcript, so I just wanted to clarify a couple of those points that the Prosecution drew my attention to. The first thing was, when we talked about the changes that you put in your statement when you were working to prepare for this testimony, and when you said that the 13th should be changed to the 14th, could you actually confirm that it was actually the other way around, that it says 14th in the statement but that the actual events, according to you, took place on the 13th? Could you please confirm that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The other change, or rather, I think it's probably a question of the interpretation, when I quoted your statement, I did it in B/C/S, and the interpretation we received did not quite correspond to the transcript in English, so I would like to read to you again the part of your testimony in English. This is page 72, lines 10 and 11. In response to a question by the Prosecutor -- "[In English] ... Mane say to you in response to that?" And your answer was: "Basically he grinned at me and he told me that the men don't need the passports anymore." So this is the part of the transcript that I was referring to. [Interpretation] Do you agree that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since we are on the topic of the passports now, from your testimony I understood that you were working on the security aspect, that your duties were security duties at Schiphol airport; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had multiple jobs or assignments on Schiphol airport, and one of them was -- or the last one was being in charge of the criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Actually, this question precedes the following question. You as any educated person know that the primary purpose of a passport is to travel abroad; is that correct? That is the main reason why a person would have a passport, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is also for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you absolutely, but the main means of identification is an identity card, in Bosnia at least, at the time when you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the Bosnian system. I only know that in the Netherlands we use either a passport or an identity card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go to the point, Mr. Lazarevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if someone does not have a passport with them but does have an identity card, that would be quite sufficient to identify that person, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions on this topic. Now I would like to go back once again to Captain Mane. We ended before the break by talking about your statement where two Serbian soldiers are mentioned. However, after this statement, you gave a statement to the Parliamentary Commission of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. On page 22, paragraph 8 of the B/C/S version, and this is on page 27, paragraph 4 of the English version, you said as follows. "[In English] Our exhibit number 4 D38, it's page 27 -- well, it's fourth paragraph. [Interpretation] I am now going to read to you what happened. In response to a question by Mrs. Huizinga-Heringa: "[In English] What was his reaction?" And your answer was: "I asked him what he was going to do with the Muslim men. He gave me the same story, that they intend interrogating them to find out whether there were any war criminals amongst them. Then I put it to him that if there are no passports, men could give false names and that the story about checking the identities would no longer be valid -- was no longer valid, sorry. He just laughed as if to say, What are you getting -- 'What are you getting so excited about? They don't need their passports anymore.' Other than that, he didn't give me any further explanation." [Interpretation] Major Van Duijn, from the answer you gave to Mrs. Huizinga-Heringa's question, it transpires that Mane didn't tell you anything but that he just laughed and that you interpreted that gesture of his in the way it is stated in your statement to the Parliamentary Commission. Very specific words were used here. "[In English] Other than that he didn't give me any further explanation." I apologise. I believe that the translation is not correct. "Other than that he didn't give me any further explanation." And we said: "He didn't say anything else to me." This is what I received on B/C/S. As if I say -- as if to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you want to go through it again for your peace of mind, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't see that much difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to do it again. Well, Your Honour, I can explain. Well, the translation that we received in B/C/S said that Mane -- "that that was everything that he told me," and here it says: "He didn't give me any further explanation other than that," and it's referring to the previous paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah, I see your point. That's why --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness obviously understood you but if the translation into B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you understood this. Based on this it transpires that he didn't actually tell you anything but that you actually interpreted his laugh or smile in the way that you did. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you look at the transcripts of the parliamentary inquiry, you could think that, but the laugh or grin from Captain Mane was if to say to me, What are you getting so excited about, full stop. "They don't need their passports anymore." That's what he said to me, and that is the only explanation he gave me. So when you read the transcripts of the parliamentary inquiry you could think there was something else, that I assumed more than that but that is not the case. I only assumed or interpreted his laugh or grin in a way to say, What are you getting so excited about? The phrase "they don't need their passports anymore," that's what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one second. This is a transcript of your hearing, so this is not -- this is a verbatim transcript of what you said; is that correct? This is not just some one conveying your words approximately.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is an exact transcript, but I was not in charge of putting the dots or the question marks in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. I would just like to go back to a question that I failed to put to you earlier. It's very brief. When you talked about your position at 02, the defensive position 02, you mentioned a group of fighters which passed by, and this is on page 38 -- [In English] Page 39 row 1 of yesterday's transcript. [Interpretation] Now I would like to just read to you what you said. [Previous translation continues] ... "[In English] ... located at 0.02 we saw a big group of men going towards Susnjari, so leaving from 0.02 towards OP Mike, so the other direction, and we could see them leaving, carrying small calibre weapons with them. Full stop. Men of all sorts of age, even young boys and old men with them." [Interpretation] I would just like to put two questions to you on this particular topic. Can you approximately say when this happened, what time did it happen?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the end of the afternoon. If I have to estimate a time it must be around 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon, late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And just so that we could have a clear situation in the transcript, what day was that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you approximately estimate the number of men that you saw there? Can you tell us an approximate number?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have to make an estimation now, somewhere around 50, between 50 and 100 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we again look at a segment of the video that we saw yesterday? This is Exhibit P02047, the segment starting from 022451 up to 022455, so it's just a few seconds of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, I think that yesterday we froze the footage at this precise frame. You recognise Mane, you recognise the interpreter Miki, and you are also in the shot. Can you see the subtitles on this frame, where they say, "And to check and see whether anybody wants to go. It's their job." Since we cannot determine from the subtitles who is saying what, whose words they are, can you please confirm the following? These words are directed by Captain Mane to the interpreter Miki, is that right, so that he could interpret them to you. Is that the right interpretation of what we are seeing here?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I saw in the video clipping, that is the correct course of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to -- a couple of seconds, I think it will be clearer. Because you hear a voice calling Miki and then it continues from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mane says to Miki to tell you that you should see whether there was anyone else who wished to leave. Does this refer to the refugees who were there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I read the subtitles, it would refer to the refugees but if I remember correctly, this phrase was not translated to me by Miki.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you. So it's more or less what's being said. But actually what I'm interested in is that you did have problems with interpretation, especially when this man named Miki was interpreting?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a way to control if Miki was telling exactly what Mane was -- wanted to tell to me because I don't speak Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. So you're saying you can't be 100 per cent sure that what Miki said was perfectly exactly interpreted by -- sorry, that what Mane said was perfectly interpreted by Miki?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have to have a way or did not have a way there to control it, but I'm sure that if things would go in a different way than Mane wanted, he would have objected and would have told Miki that he wanted it otherwise. But I don't have a way to control if it was the exact or perfect translation what Mane wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to know on this subject. On the 13th of July, 1995, in Potocari, at some point there occurred a break in the evacuation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you again a part of your testimony before the Parliamentary Commission of the Kingdom of the Netherlands [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] 24, paragraph -- well, it's 4 or 5 because there is a question again by Ms. Huizinga-Heringa. [Interpretation] The lady asked you: "Can you explain what happened exactly?" [In English] And your answer was: "After Lieutenant Rutten had tackled me, he started talking to the Serbian soldiers, in which he said, 'This is like what happened 50 years ago with the Nazis.' The Serbs got the idea that they were being branded as Nazis. They thought this was unacceptable. That was why one of them pointed out that his father had fought with the Serbian troops with Tito against the Nazis. I got Colonel Kremer to escort Lieutenant Rutten back to the camp. Then I was controlled -- confronted, sorry, by the Serbian commander asking me, 'Why do you brand us as Nazis?' The result of all this was that the transportation had to be stopped for one and a half hours. Because of this, our soldiers have to intervene because people had collapsed at temperature of about 30 degrees Celsius. This caused a lot of problems." [Interpretation] Do you stand by what you said before the Parliamentary Commission in every respect?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And at one point after this incident, and after this interruption of about 90 minutes, the evacuation resumed. On whose initiative was it resumed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Mane's initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But Major, Mane was the one who was offended and didn't want to have anything more to do with it; whereas you were the person who removed Lieutenant Rutten from the place in order to continue with the evacuation. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had Lieutenant Rutten removed from the site to prevent that things would worsen for us, but of course eventually for the refugees. So in -- the course of events was that I had Lieutenant Rutten removed. After that, had to explain to Mane and his men why this all had happened, and after that, Mane was satisfied and he decided to go on again with the process of transports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But this apology and this explanation you gave to Mane, it was aimed at continuing the evacuation, wasn't it? That was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because the stopping of the evacuation Mane ordered caused a lot of problems and people collapsing through the heat or dehydration and was causing more people to suffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do not doubt your good intentions for a moment. Anyway, the evacuation continued. But on the 13th July, the morning, before VRS soldiers arrived, between 6.00 and 8.30, let's say, you decided yourself to continue with the evacuation of refugees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You have already responded to my colleague Mr. Zivanovic that it was a convoy that included 100, 150 men. My question is this: Was there anything standing in your way if you wanted to use all the vehicles available there for the transport of men of military age, and only men, if you had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been an option but the main reason was to keep families together, and families consist of more than only men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That is also a possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now see a brief footage [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... 14, starts at 2110 and it lasts until 2116, and it bears 65 ter number P02007.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you perhaps recognise this soldier standing in front of the bus while women and children are getting in?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And does this sleeve patch mean anything to you, the one he's wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as I see it now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Major. I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau? Madam Fauveau represents General Miletic, and she will be cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, is it fair to say that during your tour in the Srebrenica enclave you were able to go on leave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it also true to say that you were able to return to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me personally, that was possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned the supplies for the DutchBat. Do you know how often there were orders made by the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't actually know whether all the convoys that were supposed to come did arrive in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from, for instance, Lieutenant Koster, that was working in the logistics branch that a lot of the convoys that were supposed to come were prevented from coming, but I don't know numbers or figures to the extent how many convoys that were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I also suppose that you don't know which items had been ordered when orders had been made.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated yesterday that you exchanged coffee against bread. Where did the coffee come from?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We still had some old amounts of coffee stacked on the OPs, which was undrinkable for us but the refugees liked it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Apart from coffee, did you exchange other items with the population?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true to say that most of the time, when you were in the enclave, you were on OPs Q and R?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main location was the compound in Potocari, and I think maybe one-third of the time I was on the OPs Quebec and Romeo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell me when you were on these two observation posts?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions, I've been there, either to resupply or to visit the two of my groups that were stationed there, so that was a weekly or two-weekly visit, and next to that I also spent multiple weeks there to stay with my troops, but I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But wasn't it the policy of the DutchBat to supply as little as possible to the people on the observation posts?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resupplying of the observation posts was hindered by the lack of fuel, and because my OPs were more or less within walking distance, of four hours, five hours, we could keep on resupplying every week or every two weeks, but other observation posts that were situated further away from the main camp were resupplied on less occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You mentioned the lack of fuel, but did the -- the UNHCR had its fuel stocked in the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the UNHCR fuel supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier on you stated that the authorisation for convoys were given on the Yellow Bridge which was close to OP P. Could you tell us who held this OP -- or, rather, who was on the Yellow Bridge where the authorisations were granted?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person that was well known figure for occupying the post we knew as Yellow Bridge was a person with the name of Jovo, but he was not in control because he was always getting through orders from a different level, and I don't know from which level or who gave Jovo orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know whether Jovo was a representative of the civilian or military authorities?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you said that the authorisations were given on the Yellow Bridge, does that mean that the convoys would arrive up to there, up to the Yellow Bridge?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard from some incidents where convoys came a long way on the route they had to take to the compound, but I don't know of a specific convoys that were stopped at Yellow Bridge or at another location, only that they were stopped somewhere along the route.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when convoys would reach the Yellow Bridge, before they did so, did they also have to cross somewhere the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the route the convoys took.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where they originated from?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned weapons and the munitions you had in the DutchBat. Page 29 you said that they were too old. Isn't it true to say that weapons and munitions were brought in together with DutchBat I into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, the weapons had been there since end of 1993 or early 1994, right?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Weren't they rather new, these weapons?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you work with weapons and you use them very intensely, and you have to maintain them, of course, when you look at the changing weather conditions, extreme weather conditions, weapons and ammunition have the tendency to reduce their usability rather fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You say that weapons and munitions were used intensively, could you tell me, if you know, whether DutchBat III or II or I did use their arms extensively and for what purposes they did, if they did?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of your firearms is more than only shooting. If you carry it with you the whole day, which was our policy, then of course the weapon is getting dirty, with sand, with other dirt, so you have to clean it, you have to oil it. The rain, the snow, the cold, the heat, everything works into the metal of the weapons. And like I said, if you carry it around you, along you with it the whole day, then they suffer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know what the life expectancy of a light weapon is?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not an expert on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you were stationed in observation post Q and R, did you have an opportunity to see the Serbian forces cross into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity myself, but I got reports from my soldiers that sometimes there were crossings of the enclave borders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It is fair to say that you had knowledge according to which Muslim forces would regularly get out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you also knew that the Muslim forces would carry out acts of sabotage and laid mines outside the enclave, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the stories the Muslim fighters told me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have contacts with the Muslim fighters, including Naser Sabanovic, and do you know which unit he was in?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had contact with Naser Sabanovic. I don't recall which unit it was, but it was the Muslim unit that was responsible for the north part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know where the HQ of the unit was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 10th and the 11th of July, when you were on this blocking position, were you able to see the Srebrenica inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could see the refugees walking alongside us or passing us on their way to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you also were able to see military men from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were the civilian population and the military mixed, as it were?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not mixed. The refugees were fleeing to the north, and at the time of the 10th and early of the 11th, the Muslim forces were -- or moving south or staying in the vicinity of the blocking positions and basically my location.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that at that time the members of the ABiH were blocking your positions and would not allow you to leave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And around that time, is that around that time that you were involved with fighting with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the 10th and the 11th, we were stationed at that blocking position, and during the whole time, there was shooting going on, so I don't know exactly what you mean with "involved with fighting with Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I will be more specific. Did you not at a given point in time shoot directly at the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain period, I gave my gunner the order to first shoot overhead if he saw forces coming over the hill, and after that, there was the intent to first shoot overhead and later on if they would not stop, shoot directly. And my gunner did that, he shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that at a certain point you left towards the compound in Srebrenica where there were refugees and where there was a climate or an atmosphere of chaos. Is it true to say that a lot of refugees were trying to climb on the UN trucks and vehicles in order to go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Next to that a lot of people were trying to leave themselves by all means or carrying their stuff themselves or using horses or donkeys to carry their personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And some of these people who were trying to climb on the UN vehicles and trucks, did they fall off the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you talk about the trucks and -- I don't know, I wouldn't know. But at a certain stage, and now I'm talking about the two APCs under my command, a few people fell off the other APC, not my APC but the other APC that was under my command. A few people fell off of that APC, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And did you know that some of the people who fell off the vehicles were run over and killed by the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge about that. And at that time, the incident I'm speaking about, that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke about the 12th of July, 1995, and you stated the men who were separated were taken to a house which had no front. Could this house be described as a house under construction?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what you define as under construction, but it was clear to me that the house had no facade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And on the 12th of July, 1995, how many men roughly did you see in that house?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th, the house with the lawn, we are speaking about then, that was the place where the men were gathered, the men that were singled out, roughly at the end of the day somewhere between 50 and 75 men were sitting on the lawn and not in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 7 D51, please. Page 7, third paragraph from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you see the last sentence in that paragraph? It reads as follows: "[In English] I saw about 15 Muslim men sitting in the house and in the garden."

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember stating this in 1995, on the 25th of October, 1995? You then stated that you had seen 15 Muslim men sitting in the house and in the garden.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember making that statement. I know that this is my statement, but you asked me to make an estimation from the top of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could it be that the estimate you gave in 1995 was closer to the truth than the estimate you now make?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the total amount of men that were around the two houses must be somewhere in the middle, between 15 and 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 13th of July the men were taken to another house, which was opposite, across the road, from the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's the house we knew as the "White House."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, the house with no facade, no front wall, and the "White House," are two separate houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that on the 12th of July you did not see men being taken to the "White House"?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see it, and it was not reported to me at the 12th either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that when you saw men being separated and when you would intervene, the men for whom you would intervene were allowed to leave with their families; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, your action had a positive influence on the men -- on the Serbs, sorry, who were trying to separate the men?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the cases I intervened, then it was clear that the men that were being singled out were too young or too old, or it was clear that they could not have been soldiers during the war. So -- and I was glad that I could -- when I intervened Mane would take over this advice and the men could stay with their families, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the night of the 12th to the 13th of July, you left to have a rest. Is that true that during the night you did not hear any major firing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the night, I was sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that the day after, in the morning of the 13th of July, when you arrived there where the refugees were, your colleague Koster told you that throughout the night there was no Serb around?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier on today you said that you proceeded to the evacuation of the population in the absence of Serbs. I'd like to know this: When the Serbs did arrive, can it be said that they had nothing against the refugees being boarded on buses, before they had arrived?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they had any objection to that. They were more surprised that we already started.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 12th of July you addressed the Serbs in order to get bread and water for the refugees?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And can it be said that the Serbs did provide bread and water afterwards?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard reports that some bread and water were provided by the Serbs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can it be said that you personally did not witness any mistreatment by the Serbs in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally see any direct mistreatment, other than I already mentioned concerning the boy that was almost strangled and the threatening of my interpreter. But other than that, there were no specific mistreatments I witnessed myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Regarding the way your interpreter was mistreated, is it right to say that it is your interpreter who reported to you the threatening words that had been addressed to him?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you, indeed, do not know at all what was said in Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no understanding of Serbo-Croatian, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that the quick evacuation of the people from Potocari was the only solution for the population?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when all the refugees were gathered at the factory sites, from that moment on, there was no other solution there than to evacuate them because, like I said before, there were -- there was a big possibility that epidemics would break out, people had no food, no water, and the temperature was very high. So from that moment on, there was no other solution, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it also correct to say that the people would rush towards the cars -- the buses, sorry, when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim people were also eager to leave, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And none of them were forced to board the buses, were they?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that, no. Other than the reports of some kicking or abusing of people that wanted to board the buses, but I have no information if that was to force them into the buses or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, you did not see any one case of a person saying they didn't want to go and they would have been forced to get into the bus?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Josse, how long do you expect to be cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 20 minutes approximately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Haynes, or Mr. Sarapa, I don't know who will --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Hard to say. I've been crossing off questions as they've gone along, but about 45 minutes at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So we are into tomorrow. So, yes, Mr. Josse, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just following on from the last set of questions that my learned friend Madam Fauveau has just asked you, it's right, isn't it, that in your original debriefing of the 13th of September, 1995, there was a pro forma question saying, treatment of civilians, refugees, and your answer was: "As far as he could tell, reasonably good." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a recollection of that. I think it's better to see the document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My apologies, I don't have the number. It was shown to you earlier and I'm about to be given it again, I'm glad to say. I'll come back to that, if I may, because in the same document, and I don't think you're going to need to see it for this purpose, you make reference to the fact that present in the enclave were two members of the British SAS, one called Jim, one called Dave, and they -- you didn't know what their orders were but you had heard that they were serving as liaison officers of sorts and that General Smith was in direct contact with them. Any recollection about that, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think you stated that you viewed -- I beg your pardon, that DutchBat viewed them as busybodies inside the unit.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few persons in the battalion staff I'd heard about, felt it like this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the information that they were there liaising directly with General Smith came from where; do you know?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of members of DutchBat crossing into Serb-held territory and, in effect, giving themselves up at about the time that the unfortunate injury to Private Van Renssen occurred?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on, then. On the 10th of July, you were in Srebrenica all day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the blocking positions, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And excuse my ignorance, does that place you in and around Bravo Company?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was under the command of Captain Groen, who was commander of the Bravo Company, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And physically, were you in and around the company headquarters?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, at the 11th, I was near the company headquarters. During the night from the 9th on the 10th, I drove to the headquarters of Captain Groen to be briefed by him and from then, went on to the blocking position. So at that time, I was further away from the company HQ that was situated in Srebrenica town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in terms of kilometres, the blocking position is how far from the town?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe, if I have to make an estimation now, maybe two, three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's where you spent most of the daylight hours of the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole time until we retreated the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions by my learned friend Mr. Lazarevic about your understanding of the position on the 12th of July as to the departure of the Muslim population of the enclave, and he asked you about whether you had any knowledge of what had gone on at the Hotel Fontana, and perhaps understandably you said you had no knowledge. Specifically, what I'd like to ask you is whether it had come through on your radio, either from Mr. Karremans or from Mr. Franken, that some sort of message had been sent by General Nikolai to the effect that the refugees needed to leave the enclave.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing was sent through the channels I had on my radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So when you started to deal with the population on the 12th of July, you had no knowledge as to what your command in Sarajevo or Tuzla was saying as to what they thought should happen to these people?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than the previous order that we could only give humanitarian aid. That was the only order that was given. Next to that, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just to be clear, that order in relation to humanitarian aid had come from whom and when, please?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had come on the morning, the early morning on the 11th through Captain Groen. Excuse me, on the early morning of the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And just, if I can press you a little further on this issue, on the 12th of July, were you receiving any orders at all from either Mr. Franken or Mr. Karremans?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was into contact with the battalion operations room, and sometimes talking to Colonel Franken, or Major Franken at the time, but no specific orders were given then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've very helpfully been provided with the document that I didn't have to hand. I can see, in fact, it bears a number, it's 7 D55. So I'm grateful to my learned friends who represent Mr. Pandurevic. It may not be on the system so let me give you the document and I'll indicate to the usher which page I'd like to go on to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can find it, 1 D31. Try it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, Your Honour, has just explained to me why it's not on the system. I think it's because he's only just received a B/C/S copy. He says he might have it on the system for tomorrow when he cross-examines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm asking that a specific page be put on the ELMO. You may want to look at the rest of the document. Yes. Can we see, it says it looks like a pro forma question, "Treatment of civilians/refugees," and your answer appears to have been, "As far as he could tell, reasonably good." I don't want to be unfair, but this appears from the debriefing to be a general question in relation to the events that you were describing and have been describing in the course of your evidence. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's a general question but it has to be seen in the light of the rest of the debriefing report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst you've got the report there, since I asked you about it, perhaps page 8 could be put on the ELMO as well, please. Little higher. Lower part of it. That's it. It's, in fact, near the redacted -- the few words that have been redacted. It's that paragraph. You said: "There were also two members of the British SAS, Jim and Dave, inside the enclave which the battalion had attached to 108." Stopping there, perhaps you should explain to the Chamber what 108 means, please.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 108 was the unit that was used for reconnaissance unit. It was a Dutch commando unit that was attached to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: "He," referring to you, "did not know what the orders of these SAS members inside the enclave were. He had heard these SAS men served as liaison officers of sorts for General Smith and were in direct contact with him. DutchBat viewed them as busybodies inside the unit." And you've already confirmed that that is the true position.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And for your information, the redacted part has been excised by the Prosecution, presumably for some immunity-type reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Josse. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I could ask two or three questions tonight or I could do it all in one piece tomorrow morning. Frankly, I would prefer the latter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we'll make that sacrifice, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very, very kind of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, you'll be in the witness box tomorrow for approximately 40, 45 minutes and then you will be free to go. And basically that means, Mr. McCloskey, you'll have the next witness lined up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to tell you, Your Honour, we have been going on the basis of the estimates and that witness is a bit of a ways from here, and so he would have had to have here tonight and we did not have him available. I've been speaking to the Defence. They are happy -- well, they were happy to have the time to prepare for him over the holiday but we did not have him. We were -- weren't expecting it to end this quickly. I apologise.
